name: Ser Darrow of Edgemoor
appearance: Thirty-two, tall and rangy, with short dark hair that won't lie flat, a few days of dark stubble and grey-green eyes in a lean, weathered face. His nose was broken once and set a little crooked, with a faint scar across the bridge; his smile comes out dry and lopsided, and his laugh carries the length of a hall. At Saint Ysolde's he wears a plain linen infirmary shirt, often with a grey wool blanket round his shoulders, and gets up the way he does everything now: the good leg first, then the bad one, then the slow transfer, as if crossing a frozen pond. This week he walks the length of the hall without the stick, and he does not limp.
portrait_alt: Portrait of Ser Darrow: a man in his thirties with short dark hair, stubble, a nose once broken and set a little crooked, and a dry half-smile, a grey wool blanket around his shoulders over a linen shirt, in a stone infirmary hall with a fire on one side and a snowy mountain window on the other.
last_seen_doing: On his own cot, having won the stone at knucklebones and heard what Hollis had meant to tell somebody: two days dry, three by the dusk bell.
now: Seven weeks past the Binding, in the season Maelis says is the softest. He sat in Mother Ione's council in the warming room, heard the law of Old Mercy (while it rings at dawn and dusk, no blade climbs the Steps or passes the gate), and asked to be sent down on the cage before the grey cloaks arrive; Maelis said no for the fifteenth time. Rae Thorne has asked whether he rode a grey at the ford and gone up the stair without saying why, and the Prior, before she decides whether the bell rings, has asked him what she ought to know and what the lay brothers should tell the valley. Back at his cot he won the stone at knucklebones from Hollis, and the story told true that Hollis paid was that he is two days without a drink and had not known who to tell.
story_so_far: With the Grace of the field-stone warm in his chest and sixty knights behind him, Darrow led the Ninth Lance into the Wend at Harrow Ford, laughing, until halfway across the warmth went out of him, his horse went down, and his knee gave with nothing touching it as he planted and turned toward the boy who had gone under his horse. As he went under he saw Aldric Vane's horse on the west bank, already turned and climbing out, one heartbeat early. A red-handed clanswoman hauled him onto the east bank by his collar and made him look: the Wend carrying knights downstream, the Second Lance sitting untouched on the far shore, and a line of grey armored figures standing very still under the trees. Nineteen of the Ninth came home, and the Crown's heralds were already on the bell-house steps naming them the Faithless and bidding them kneel anew at the Oathspire. Carried up the Thousand Steps to the House of Menders, he chose Maelis Vorne's old art over the Crown's fast way, a strand of his own sinew bound in with emberthread, nothing given and nothing anyone can take back, and heard that he may never kneel again. Seven weeks on, walking without the stick, he learns that six grey cloaks with a cart and a censer are riding the Holloway toward the foot of the Steps with a list of the Faithless, and that when Wren was asked who was first on it, she looked at him.

quote.text: I was never much good at it anyway.

known_facts.fact: He captains the Ninth Lance, sixty knights and sixty squires, and has the fastest feet in the Lowmarch, having never once cared whose father mattered.
He and Aldric Vane rode knee to knee from the time they were squires and were knighted the same morning in the same cold chapel, palms on the warming Oathstone.
Before the charge he read the clan line as fleeing something in the trees behind them, coming through the ford rather than at it, and Hollis Garrow answered that the writ said clear the ford.

Halfway across the Wend the Grace went out of him in a single heartbeat, frost bloomed on his mail in midsummer, and when he planted his left foot and turned toward Tobin Marsh the knee gave with no blade and nothing touching it.
As he went under he saw Aldric's horse on the west bank already turned and climbing out, one heartbeat early.
The red-handed woman dragged him by the collar of his gambeson to the east bank among the standing stones, turned his head to the river, and told him in rough Vaelish to look and remember it.
Nineteen of the Ninth came back from Harrow Ford; he made himself count them, and he knows the names of the other forty-one and does not say them.

The surgeons of the Lowmarch pressed the knee, watched it slide, and sent him north, and four lay brothers carried him up the Thousand Steps on a litter, feverish, while Wren Ashdown counted the steps aloud beside him and insisted there are eleven hundred and seventeen.

The last of the road to the foot of the Steps was in a salt-cart driven by a woman the lay brothers called Rae, whom he watched because the fever had taken away his choice of what to watch, and would have watched without it; she talked to her oxen and not to her passengers, looked at his leg once the way a carter looks at a cracked wheel, and told him as they lifted him that they would count him up and he should not help.

Maelis Vorne found the cord in the middle of the knee snapped rather than broken, and when he said it had held for thirty-two years she answered that it had help for twelve of them, and would not explain.
Offered the Crown's way or the Binding, he chose the Binding, an art the Crown burned the knowers of three hundred years ago, and was told he may not kneel for a long time, perhaps not ever.
A list of the Faithless at Saint Ysolde's was read out at the inn in Coldmere; Hollis Garrow is second on it, and when Hollis asked who was first, Wren did not answer and looked at Darrow.

From the infirmary window he knew the cart standing at the winch-house at the foot of the Steps, shafts up and two oxen in the snow, as the one he had ridden the last of the Holloway in, and he had not forgotten the one thing its driver said to him.

At the infirmary window the Reckoning showed itself to him for the first time, a pale gold script hanging over his palms that he could read though nobody had learned it in three hundred years, and behind his own numbers stood fainter ones whose owner he did not need to be told.
known_facts.evidence: He could read it anyway, and it was reading him

known_facts.fact: While Hollis hid the writ, the Captain was shut in a cell down the hall with Mender Vorne and nothing came through the door; Hollis has thought for a fortnight that a man could fight sitting down, if somebody taught him to stop looking at the floor.

Behind the cell door, Maelis told him of two fires a man can carry: one poured in, which the hand that poured it can take back, and one built by his own work, which cannot be poured or taken; the script he saw counts only the built one.
He knew the name of the burned order before she said it, from the curse the lowlands make of it, and she forbade him to say it in the hall, to Wren, to the Prior, or to Hollis most of all.

He argued that Hollis, second on the list and lying on his back when it is read, was owed the knowing of the built fire before he was; Maelis answered that Hollis is owed a leg and will get a wooden one, and that when Hollis asks, Darrow will lie to him. He took it.

He asked Hollis and Benedek why the Confessors chase the Faithless up a mountain if the Grace left them for faithlessness, and why mercy needs a list with his name first; he kept what Maelis told him behind his teeth.
Asked what the Grace did, he told Maelis: it made the river a road and every ache go quiet, and when it went it was cold, frost on his mail in midsummer. Asked whether he broke his oath, he said no.

He told Maelis the Grace did not go but was taken, since sixty men do not lose a thing in the same heartbeat by accident; she agreed that then somebody took it, and said that what it did at the ford, and whose doing, she does not know.
known_facts.evidence: Sixty men don't lose a thing in the same heartbeat by accident

known_facts.fact: At Mother Ione's council he saw Sister Pell's cup chatter on the hearth before it settled, and read it before he meant to, the way he read a line before a charge; nobody else looked.
known_facts.evidence: He read it before he meant to, the way he read a line before a charge. Nobody else looked.

known_facts.fact: Asked by Rae Thorne on the stair whether he rode a grey at the ford, he said yes and asked why; she did not say. He has not said Thistle's name since the river.
known_facts.evidence: He had not said her name since

known_facts.fact: At the council he asked to be put on the cage with the next load down before the grey cloaks reached the foot of the Steps, so the list would have nothing to climb for. Maelis answered for the fifteenth time, to the fire: the thread is soft, eleven hundred steps down are eleven hundred chances to tear it, and the cage is for salt. Rae said that down is where they are.

Back from the council he read Hollis's hands as he had read Sister Pell's cup, asked once about them, was put off, and played him at knucklebones for a story told true; he caught the stone on the back of his hand, and Hollis paid: two days without a drink, three by the dusk bell.
known_facts.evidence: The bone sat on Darrow's knuckles

known_facts.fact: His answer, when Hollis said he had not known who to tell: that he had told the one man on the mountain who could not buy him a drink.
known_facts.evidence: the one man on this mountain who can't buy you a drink

relationships.label: his Mender
relationships.note: She tied the Binding with a strand of his own sinew and emberthread, reads the Knots with two fingers and her eyes shut, has told him fifteen times he may not go down the Steps, and it is she who will make him be honest, later, about how much he loved the charge.

relationships.label: of the Sixth Lance, on the next cot
relationships.note: He waved the writ at Darrow on the west bank and told him his head was not as fast as his feet; lost his right leg above the knee at the ford, cursed Darrow among many others on the carts north, and snores on his right at Saint Ysolde's, second on the list where Wren, asked who was first, only looked at Darrow.

relationships.label: the girl with the ledger who counted him up the Steps
relationships.note: She counted the steps aloud beside his litter and would not let him say she had missed one; it was she who brought word of the grey cloaks, and who looked at him when Hollis asked whose name was first.

relationships.label: knighted the same morning
relationships.note: Squires together, knighted the same morning; at the ford Aldric told him to ride wider and seemed about to say more, and Darrow saw his horse already turned on the west bank; Darrow believes it was Aldric's hand that wrote his name first on the Confessors' list.

relationships.label: the youngest of the Ninth
relationships.note: Nineteen, who sang badly and constantly; when Tobin went under his own horse in the current, Darrow came off his mare and turned toward him, and that turn is where the knee went.

relationships.label: the woman who pulled him out
relationships.note: She looked at him alone across the water before the charge and called something the river took; afterward she hauled him to the east bank, made him look at what the Wend was carrying, and was gone when he turned back; he did not see her again for a long time.

relationships.label: the carter who drove him the last of the road
relationships.note: She talked to her oxen and not to him, looked at his leg once like a cracked wheel, and said one thing to him all day; seven weeks after the Binding he knew her cart at the winch-house from the window, and Wren says it was she who heard the list read and climbed through the night to bring it up.
